name: Contouring and highlighting (1970s origin)

card.summary: A makeup technique that uses darker shades in hollows and lighter shades on high points to make the face look more sculpted, slimmer or more defined.
card.note: Histories trace the technique to theatre and 1940s film makeup and a 1990s-2010s revival; a specific 1970s origin is not documented.

quick.overview:
Contouring places a shade one or two tones darker than the skin in the hollows of the cheeks, along the sides of the nose and at the temples, and highlighting places a lighter shade on prominent areas such as the cheekbones, nose tip and T-zone. The shadow slims and the highlight draws the eye, so the face looks more defined.

The idea comes from stage and film makeup: Elizabethan actors used chalk and soot, and Max Factor added shading for film in the 1920s and 1930s. Makeup artist Kevyn Aucoin's 2000 book Face Forward is credited with bringing contouring to the public, and Kim Kardashian and affordable brands made it widespread in the 2010s.
quick.how: People apply contour and highlight products, such as creams, sticks or powders, with brushes or sponges and blend the edges into the foundation. Practitioners adapt placement to face shape, using shading to slim or reshape and highlight to emphasise features.
quick.risks: Makeup carries the usual cosmetic risks of skin irritation or breakouts from products. The effect is temporary and wears off with removal.

lead: Contouring and highlighting is a makeup technique that uses shadow and light to reshape how the face looks. Darker shades go where a person wants to create hollows or slim an area, such as under the cheekbones, along the nose and at the temples, and lighter shades go on features to be brought forward, such as cheekbones, nose tip and the centre of the forehead [1].

The approach is rooted in theatre and film. Wikipedia notes Elizabethan actors using chalk and soot to make expressions readable, greasepaint after electric stage lighting arrived, shading by Marlene Dietrich in films, and Max Factor Sr. adding shading so faces would not look flat on screen, with a 1945 tutorial on contouring for different face shapes [1].

The technique reached the general public through Kevyn Aucoin's 2000 book Face Forward and the 2010s, when Kim Kardashian and affordable brands popularised it [1]. Histories of the technique trace it to theatre and 1940s film makeup; a distinct 1970s origin is not documented in the Wikipedia account.

chain: Apply darker shade to hollows and lighter shade to high points
Shadow recedes areas and highlight brings others forward
Face looks slimmer, with stronger cheekbones and nose lines
angle.text: Contouring changes the visual impression of face shape for as long as the makeup is worn. Users aim for stronger cheekbones, a slimmer face or a narrower nose.

paras: Contour shade is described as warm or cool and one or two tones darker than the skin, placed in the cheek hollows, along the sides of the nose and on the temples. Highlighter, one or two tones lighter, goes on the apples of the cheeks, nose tip and T-zone [1]. Strobing is a related approach using only lighter shades [1].

The darker shading creates shadow with a slimming effect, while highlight draws attention to raised areas, so the technique can accentuate the face's structure or play down features a person wants to de-emphasise [1].

Stage makeup in the 16th century used chalk and soot, followed by greasepaint in the late 1800s as electric stage lighting spread [1]. Film-era shading developed in the 1920s and 1930s, and Max Factor Sr. presented a tutorial on contouring for different face shapes in 1945 [1]. Subtle contouring was common among 1950s Hollywood actresses [1].

Kevyn Aucoin was largely responsible for the sculpted look of many celebrities and models in the 1990s, and his 2000 book Face Forward introduced sculpting and contouring to the general public [1]. In the 2010s, Kim Kardashian and others spread it further, and low-cost brands began selling contour products [1]. Drag performers also use it to emphasise feminine features [1].
